outcome: As of 11 October 2026 the question remains open: no event since 26 January 2024 settles termination of the odd greedy expansion for all rationals with odd denominator, and the only in-window result specific to the odd greedy expansion (Louwsma and Martino, Integers 2025) classifies rationals whose odd greedy expansion has exactly two terms.
problem_asks: Part 1, the objects: every rational number with an odd denominator. The statement does not say positive, but the greedy procedure is defined only for positive rationals, so the scope is implicitly positive rationals with odd denominator. Part 2, the procedure: the odd greedy expansion, i.e. repeatedly subtract the largest unit fraction 1/u with u odd and 1/u not exceeding the current remainder, on odd-denominator unit fractions only. Part 3, the claim: each such rational has an odd greedy expansion, meaning the procedure reaches remainder 0 after finitely many steps, so the rational is a finite sum of distinct odd-denominator unit fractions produced by the greedy rule. Nothing else is asked; the existence of some all-odd Egyptian representation (Breusch 1954) is a different question and is not what the bullet asks.

events.what_happened: R. Breusch, solution to Advanced Problem 4512 (posed by E. P. Starke, 1952), American Mathematical Monthly 61 (1954), 200-201: every x/y with y odd has an Egyptian fraction representation with all denominators odd. The proof does not use the greedy procedure. Some secondary sources credit B. M. Stewart (American Journal of Mathematics 76 (1954), 779-785, titled 'Sums of distinct divisors') jointly; the Stewart paper was not read. Original Breusch paper not opened; known here from secondary sources (Louwsma and Martino arXiv 2309.07280, opened).
events.delivers: Existence only: every rational with odd denominator is a finite sum of distinct odd-denominator unit fractions. Does not establish that the greedy rule produces such a sum, so it does not touch termination of the odd greedy procedure.
events.remains: Termination of the odd greedy procedure for every rational with odd denominator (all of problem_asks).
events.direction: Points to existence of odd representations, not to the greedy claim; it answers a neighbouring question (existence without greedy).

events.what_happened: Stan Wagon, emails of October 1996, reported on the Eppstein page: the odd greedy run on 3/179 finished after 19 terms, the last denominator having 439,492 digits; the remainder numerators ran 3 through 17, then 2, 3, 4, 1. Wagon wrote that 'it is a famous open question whether ODD GREEDY always halts'. Source read: Eppstein's page 'Egyptian Fractions - Odd Greediness and 3/179', which quotes the emails.
events.delivers: One finite instance: the odd greedy expansion of 3/179 terminates after 19 terms. This is one more terminating rational; it does not move the universal claim.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: termination for every rational with odd denominator.
events.directly_checkable: The 19 terms can be checked by exact arithmetic in principle, but the last denominator has 439,492 digits, so checking needs modular methods; Eppstein's page describes the modular approach used for later examples.
events.doubts: Eppstein's own program did not finish 3/179 in a reasonable time (November 1997, same page), and no 1997 run reproduced Wagon's 1996 finish on that page. The 1996 run is reported in emails, not a paper.
events.direction: Consistent with termination for this one rational. Says nothing about the universal claim.
events.object: The odd greedy expansion of 3/179: 19 distinct odd unit fractions summing to 3/179, the last with a 439,492-digit denominator. Explicit (computed), not existential. Illustrates how long terminating expansions can be.

events.what_happened: Late 1997 computations reported on Eppstein's 3/179 page: David Bailey's exhaustive search rediscovered 3/2879 (reported finished, last term about 3,000,000 digits, 4 November 1997) and 5/5809 (27 terms; Eppstein's modular computation showed it halts after 27 terms, numerators 5 through 30 then 1, 1 December 1997). Bailey ran 5/3809 to 50,000,000 digits without halting (9 November 1997); Milo Gardner later reported 60,000,000 digits with no halt. K. S. Brown is credited with independently finding 5/5809 (Wikipedia's odd greedy article, opened). Dates are as given on the Eppstein page; day-level detail was not checked against the emails.
events.delivers: Further finite instances (3/2879, 5/5809) and non-halting observations for 5/3809 up to 5 x 10^7 digits. None of these is evidence either way for the universal claim, since a computation stopped at a digit count does not show non-termination.
events.directly_checkable: 5/5809 (27 terms) is checkable by modular arithmetic using the modulus Bailey gave (6(31!)(10!)(6!)(4!)^2), per the MathPages source (opened, undated).
events.doubts: Non-halting at a digit count is not non-termination. Eppstein disputed Helaman Ferguson's suggestion (December 1997) that long expansions arise near even-denominator fractions, and Eppstein's heuristic (numerators falling on average) was cast in doubt by these runs, per the same page.
events.direction: Instance-level: terminating examples and unfinished runs. Neither direction is a verdict on the universal claim.
events.object: 5/5809: odd greedy expansion of 27 terms, remainder numerators rising by one from 5 to 30 and then 1 (computed via modular arithmetic). 3/2879: finished, last term about 3 million digits (computed).

events.what_happened: Jukka Pihko, 'Remarks on the Greedy Odd Egyptian Fraction Algorithm', Fibonacci Quarterly 39(3), 2001. Per a search-result summary, it classifies steps of the odd greedy algorithm as 'good' (numerator decreases) or 'bad' (numerator increases). A 1999 Pihko paper is also said (search summary) to list termination as open. The PDF was not readable with my tools (binary output), so these statements are unverified.
events.delivers: Not established: the paper could not be read. Per the search summary it classifies steps; it is not known to state a termination result.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, as far as I could establish.
events.doubts: Content unverified; PDF unreadable in my tools.
events.direction: Not established.

events.what_happened: Jukka Pihko, 'Remarks on the Greedy Odd Egyptian Fraction Algorithm II', Fibonacci Quarterly 48(3) (2010), 202-208. Per the abstract text in a search result: for an odd prime p and 1 < a < p there are infinitely many odd b for which the numerator sequence of the odd greedy algorithm runs a, a+1, ..., p-1, 1. The PDF was not readable with my tools; the abstract statement is from the search result, not from the paper.
events.delivers: A structural family of denominators with a prescribed numerator pattern. It does not establish termination for any rational outside that construction.
events.doubts: Abstract text from a search result only; paper unread.
events.direction: Structural; it cuts neither way on the universal claim.

events.what_happened: Christian Elsholtz, 'Egyptian Fractions with odd denominators', arXiv:1606.02117 (submitted 7 June 2016). Bounds the number of solutions of sum 1/x_i = 1 in distinct odd positive integers. No greedy procedure. Discarded: a counting result about a different question.
events.revisions: One version (v1) per arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: Counts solutions of sum 1/x_i = 1 with odd distinct x_i. Not about expansions of a given rational, and not about the greedy rule.
events.direction: Not about this problem.

events.what_happened: Hung Viet Chu, 'A Threshold for the Best Two-term Underapproximation by Egyptian Fractions', arXiv:2306.12564 (v1 19 June 2023; v2 20 January 2024). Concerns the ORDINARY greedy expansion G(p/q): Theorem 1.12 says that for odd q with Upsilon(p,q)=2 the partial sums of G(p/q) are the unique best m-term underapproximations for every m. A search summary had described this as concerning the odd greedy expansion; the text I read defines G as the ordinary greedy expansion, so it is not the odd greedy expansion. Discarded as a different expansion. The arXiv HTML was read through its first 100,000 of about 110,000 characters.
events.revisions: v1 19 Jun 2023; v2 20 Jan 2024 (the v2 date is before the frozen revision).
events.delivers: For the ordinary greedy Egyptian expansion, best two-term underapproximation under Upsilon(p,q) <= 2 with q odd. A different expansion and a different question. Says nothing about termination of the odd greedy procedure.
events.direction: Not about this problem: the object studied is the ordinary greedy expansion.

events.what_happened: Joel Louwsma and Joseph Martino, 'Rational numbers with odd greedy expansion of fixed length', arXiv:2309.07280, v1 13 September 2023 (the only version listed). Determines all reduced fractions with fixed numerator n whose odd greedy expansion has length 2; for length m, all rationals whose odd greedy expansion has length m and begins with m-1 prescribed odd denominators; and an infinite family when m-2 denominators are prescribed. The abstract says: 'It is an open question whether this expansion always has finitely many terms.' Acknowledgements (read via ar5iv): Nathan Kaplan suggested studying the odd greedy algorithm; Claire Levaillant; funding from Niagara University. No AI disclosure.
events.revisions: v1 only (13 Sep 2023), per arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: Classifies rationals with odd greedy expansions of prescribed shape: fixed numerator with length 2, or prescribed leading denominators with length m. Each case is a finite-length family; the paper states termination in general is open. Restricted families only.
events.remains: Termination of the odd greedy expansion for every rational with odd denominator (all of problem_asks).
events.direction: Restricted classifications; no direction on the universal claim.

events.what_happened: Joel Louwsma and Joseph Martino, 'Rational Numbers with Two-Term Odd Greedy Expansion', Integers 25 (2025). The abstract line 'We find all rational numbers whose odd greedy expansion has two terms' is quoted in a search result. The journal publication date 28 May 2025 and the received/revised/accepted dates (20 May 2024, 30 Jan 2025, 22 Apr 2025) are from front matter quoted in a search result; I could not read the PDF (binary output), so these dates are unverified by me. The earlier arXiv version (2309.07280) is dated September 2023, so the first public written argument on the two-term classification may be earlier than the journal date if a preprint of this paper exists; I found none. The journal date is therefore recorded as the earliest date I could establish.
events.revisions: Received 20 May 2024; revised 30 Jan 2025; accepted 22 Apr 2025; published 28 May 2025 (per search-result front matter, unverified by me). No arXiv version found.
events.delivers: Classifies every rational whose odd greedy expansion has exactly two terms. This is a classification of a finite-length sub-family (every rational in it terminates after two steps). It sets no bound on lengths and says nothing about rationals outside the family, so it does not establish termination in general.
events.remains: Termination of the odd greedy expansion for every rational with odd denominator; expansions of length other than two.

events.what_happened: Vjekoslav Kovac, 'On eventually greedy best underapproximations by Egyptian fractions', arXiv:2406.07218 (v1 11 June 2024; v2 13 June 2024; v3 26 September 2024). Shows that the set of reals for which the best n-term Egyptian underapproximations are eventually greedy has Lebesgue measure zero, answering a question of Erdos and Graham (listed as Erdos problem 206 per a search result). Neighbouring question; abstract page read, full text not read.
events.revisions: v1 11 Jun 2024; v2 13 Jun 2024; v3 26 Sep 2024 (current).
events.delivers: A measure-zero statement about reals under the best-underapproximation property. Different question: no odd denominators and no odd greedy expansion.
events.direction: Not about this problem.

events.what_happened: Zheng Li and Quanyu Tang, 'On a conjecture of Erdos and Graham about the Sylvester's sequence', arXiv:2503.12277 (v1 15 March 2025; v4 21 March 2025 is the version shown). Resolves an Erdos-Graham liminf conjecture on Sylvester's sequence; a generalisation is conditional on the unproven Erdos-Graham claim that every rational has eventually greedy best Egyptian underapproximations. Neighbouring question; abstract page read only.
events.revisions: v1 15 Mar 2025; v2 18 Mar 2025; v3 20 Mar 2025; v4 21 Mar 2025 (per arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: A result on Sylvester's sequence and its liminf. Not about odd denominators or the odd greedy expansion.
events.direction: Not about this problem.

Egyptian fraction solutions whose denominators' prime factors lie in a fixed set; evaluates the greedy algorithm for bounds. The abstract page never mentions odd denominators or the odd greedy expansion. Discarded.
events.revisions: One version (v1), per arXiv abstract page.
events.delivers: Bounds on Egyptian fraction solutions with prime factors constrained; the greedy algorithm is used for bounds. Not about odd denominators or the odd greedy expansion.
events.direction: Not about this problem.

events.revisions: v1 14 Feb 2024; v2 8 Jul 2024; v3 20 Jan 2025 (per arXiv abstract page).

events.what_happened: google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/282.lean (copyright 2025). Lean statements of Erdos problem 282: theorem erdos_282 says that for x in (0,1) with odd denominator, the greedy remainder using A = odd numbers is eventually 0, with proof 'sorry'. Variants: general (open, answer placeholder), fibonacci (A = all naturals, proof 'sorry'), graham (iff with answer placeholder, proof 'sorry'), sq (square denominators, proof 'sorry'). The only proved declarations are test lemmas. The formal file was read through a text reader; exact dates of the file's commits were not established.
events.revisions: Copyright year 2025 in file header; later commits not checked.
events.delivers: A formal statement of the odd-denominator question, restricted to x in (0,1). Not a proof: the main theorem is sorry-marked.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, since no proof is present. Note that the formal statement restricts x to (0,1) while the Wikipedia wording does not.
events.direction: Formal statement only; no direction.

events.what_happened: Forum comment on Erdos problem 282 on erdosproblems.com by user Vjeko_Kovac, dated 11 August 2025 (per a fetch summary of the thread; the comment was not read verbatim). Sketches, non-constructively, that there exist sets A asymptotically equal to the squares for which the greedy process does not terminate, via an observation on Problem 263. The author says they are 'still undecided' whether this helps with the concrete questions. Concerns the square-denominator variant, not odd denominators.
events.delivers: A sketched claim about a variant (A asymptotic to the squares). It does not address the odd-number version.
events.doubts: A forum sketch; the author says undecided about the concrete questions; not written up as a paper; read through a fetch summary, not verbatim.
events.direction: Would cut against termination for a square-denominator variant, not for the odd-number question.

events.what_happened: Forum thread on Erdos problem 282: comment by user trajenta, 7 July 2026, notes that the algorithm as written does not exclude reusing denominators (for x = 2/3 with odd numbers it gives 2/3 = 1/3 + 1/3). Thomas Bloom (maintainer of erdosproblems.com) replied the same day that the intended rule is to choose the largest unit fraction, with denominator in the target set, not yet used. Clarifies the convention; claims no result.
events.delivers: Nothing new mathematically; clarifies that the odd-number version uses distinct unit fractions, largest available at each step.

checked_by.qualification: Maintainer of erdosproblems.com; listed as Thomas F. Bloom (University of Manchester) in the FrontierMath Erdos paper (arXiv 2609.25050)
checked_by.what_they_did: Replied in the forum thread clarifying the intended convention (largest unused unit fraction). Not a verification of the problem's answer.

events.direction: No direction: a scope clarification.

events.what_happened: Samuel Korsky, 'Approximating 1 by Sums of Unit Fractions', arXiv:2607.04157 (v1 5 July 2026; v2 8 October 2026). Improves an Erdos-Graham bound on how close a subset sum of a large collection of unit fractions can get to 1 from below. Not about odd denominators or greedy expansions. Discrepancy: a search result listed the same arXiv ID under the title 'A Stretched-Exponential Bound for an Erdos--Graham Unit-Fraction Problem' with a sentence saying the author was assisted by GPT-5.5 Pro. The current abstract page shows a different title and no AI sentence, and I did not open the full text. Unresolved.
events.revisions: v1 5 Jul 2026; v2 8 Oct 2026 (per arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: A bound on subset sums of unit fractions near 1. Not about odd denominators or the odd greedy expansion.
events.direction: Not about this problem.

events.what_happened: Vjekoslav Kovac and Quanyu Tang, 'Eventually greedy best Egyptian underapproximations of rational numbers via optimal control', arXiv:2607.28387 (v1 30 July 2026; v2 4 August 2026). Proves every positive rational has eventually greedy best Egyptian underapproximations, both with repeated and with distinct denominators; answers an Erdos-Graham problem as relayed by the abstract, and constructs an irrational answering a Nathanson question. NEIGHBOURING QUESTION: not about odd denominators or the odd greedy expansion. The paper's 'Declaration of AI usage' (read via the arXiv HTML page through a text reader) credits OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol with key steps in the proof of Theorem 1 and with Figure 1, and says ChatGPT was used in two conversations (one reported it could not solve the problem; the other produced a candidate approach, which was then organised into a draft). The authors say they rewrote the material and that final statements and proofs were written by the authors. Recorded here as an AI-involvement event for a neighbouring result, not for this problem. Quotes are from a text reader and should be checked character for character against the PDF.
events.revisions: v1 30 Jul 2026 (27 KB); v2 4 Aug 2026 (30 pages). Per the arXiv abstract page, v2 comments say Theorem 4, Figure 1, Remark 6 and Section 4 were added after discussions with colleagues.
events.delivers: Every positive rational has eventually greedy best Egyptian underapproximations (repeated and distinct denominators). The restriction is to the best-underapproximation property of the greedy expansion; it does not involve odd denominators. The word 'odd' appears only in an unrelated condition in the introduction (per the first pass of the text reader).
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the odd greedy termination question is untouched.
events.doubts: Not assessed as a claim about this problem. Only the authors' declaration is recorded; no reviews or verifications found.
events.direction: Not about this problem. For its own question it answers the greedy best underapproximation problem affirmatively for all positive rationals.

events.what_happened: Google DeepMind's AlphaProof Nexus (preprint, May 2026; sources give 21 May and 26 May, so day is uncertain). The public repository google-deepmind/alphaproof-nexus-results lists erdos_282, erdos_282.variants.graham and erdos_282.variants.sq in erdos_problems_attempted.txt (353 entries in total). The published proof folders (APNOutputs/ErdosProblems and NaturalLanguageProofs/ErdosProblems) show nine problems: erdos_12 (parts i and ii), erdos_125 (positive_lower_density variant), erdos_138 (difference variant), erdos_152, erdos_26 (tenenbaum variant), erdos_741 (parts i and ii), erdos_846. Neither folder shows 282. The DeepMind coverage says 9 of 353 open problems were solved. Recorded as an AI attempt that has no published proof for 282 in the visible listings.
events.delivers: No result for this problem. The visible public outputs show no published AlphaProof Nexus proof for problem 282 or its variants; the attempt itself is recorded in the attempted list only.
events.doubts: The folder listings end in 'View all files', so a 282 proof file could exist beyond the visible list; I did not open individual proof files. The README says the results repository 'contains only problems where successful proofs were discovered by AlphaProof Nexus', which is consistent with 282 having no success, but I did not confirm that from a file.
events.direction: No claimed direction. Attempted, with no published proof visible.

disputes.summary: Attribution of the odd-denominator problem varies by source. The Erdos problem 282 page credits the odd case to Stein (and Fibonacci for the unrestricted case). A search summary of the Wikipedia article credits Stein, Selfridge, Graham and others and cites Guy (1981). Louwsma and Martino (2023) attribute the open question to Guy (Section D11) and Klee and Wagon (Problem 15). The Erdos-Graham 1980 p. 30 attribution is unverified. No competing priority claims found.

Breusch (1954) is credited alone in some sources and jointly with Stewart (1954, American Journal of Mathematics) in others for the existence of all-odd Egyptian representations. The Stewart paper was not read.

summary: No event since 26 January 2024 settles, or moves, the universal question for odd greedy expansions. Wikipedia's live list (number theory, computational number theory) still carries the bullet verbatim without a reference; the odd greedy article's last edit is 28 May 2024 and it still calls the problem open. erdosproblems.com #282 asks the same question (with A equal to the odd numbers); its page, history and forum show no claimed solution, one convention clarification on 7 July 2026, and an unverified sketch on a square-denominator variant (August 2025). The in-window result specific to the odd greedy expansion is Louwsma and Martino's classification of rationals whose odd greedy expansion has exactly two terms (Integers 25, 2025). Their 2023 preprint classifies fixed-numerator and fixed-length cases and says termination is open. Both are finite-length families, so they are restricted cases, not the universal claim. Close call: a pass could read the length-two classification as a set of newly confirmed instances growing (section 2.1) rather than a restricted case; I record it as a classification of a terminating sub-family and leave the call. The Integers PDF was unreadable in my tools (binary output), so its statement, acknowledgements, AI disclosure and exact dates rest on search-result front matter and quotations, not on my reading of the paper. Pre-window computations (Wagon 1996; Bailey, Eppstein and Brown 1997) show terminating long expansions (3/179 in 19 terms, 5/5809 in 27 terms) and non-halting runs at digit counts; they are instances, not evidence either way. AI involvement: none found for this problem. The AlphaProof Nexus preprint (May 2026) lists erdos_282, erdos_282.variants.graham and erdos_282.variants.sq among its 353 attempted problems, but the visible published proof folders list nine other problems and not 282; the Tao AI-contributions wiki (data to 30 June 2026) has no row for 282; the Lean formalisation (DeepMind formal-conjectures) has erdos_282 with a sorry proof; FrontierMath Erdos (6 Sept 2026; 68 open problems as of Aug 2026) does not include 282 (per its appendix as summarised by a reader). I also searched for GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, Aristotle, Gemini Deep Think and Mathoverflow in connection with this problem and found nothing. The one AI-credited paper in the neighbourhood is Kovac and Tang (arXiv 2607.28387, 30 July 2026), which answers a different question and whose own declaration credits GPT-5.6 Sol with key steps of its Theorem 1 and ChatGPT with a candidate approach and a draft. It is recorded as a neighbour event, not as AI involvement in this problem. Scope notes for the judging pass: the Lean and Erdos 282 statements restrict x to (0,1), whereas Wikipedia's wording is 'every rational number with an odd denominator' (positivity implicit); the Erdos page asks the odd question as a special case of a general question about which pairs (x, A) terminate, which is not part of this bullet. Corrections to search summaries: Chu's Theorem 1.12 concerns the ordinary greedy expansion, not odd greedy; the Korsky arXiv ID now carries a different title from the one a search result showed with a GPT-5.5 Pro sentence, which I could not resolve.
competing_reading: Read as an affirmative signal: the odd greedy procedure has been proved to terminate for an infinite family of rationals (all with length-two expansions, Louwsma and Martino 2025), terminates for every long example checked (Wikipedia: all instances tested), and Erdos problem 282 has no claimed counterexample. On that reading the 2025 classification is progress on the problem's own quantity (the set of rationals with finite odd greedy expansions) and a pass could count it as an advance rather than a restricted case. The stronger reading against: terminating families and computed instances never reach the universal claim (section 2.1; the Collatz analogy), and the one 'non-halting' case (3/179 in Eppstein's 1997 program; 5/3809 at 5 x 10^7 digits) is unresolved, so the problem is no closer to settled on the evidence recorded here.
what_would_settle_it: A published proof of termination for every rational with odd denominator, or an explicit rational whose odd greedy run is shown never to halt; failing that, a readable copy of Louwsma and Martino (Integers 25, 2025) to confirm the statement, the acknowledgements and any AI disclosure, and the exact first public date; the full AlphaProof Nexus file listing (with the 'View all files' view) to confirm that no erdos_282 proof file exists; and the verbatim PDF text of arXiv 2607.28387 to confirm the declaration's sentences, which I read through a text reader.

judgement.why: The statement asks whether the odd greedy procedure halts for every odd-denominator rational. No event proves termination for any independently defined class of rationals or exhibits a non-halting one. The closest call is Louwsma–Martino 2025 (and its 2023 preprint): classifying which rationals have two-term (or prescribed-shape) odd greedy expansions characterises rationals already known to terminate rather than establishing termination for a restriction of the question, so I scored it variant rather than case; the competing reading (an infinite terminating family as a case) was weighed and rejected because the family is defined by terminating. Computations of 3/179, 5/5809 etc. are instances. Breusch, Elsholtz, Chu, Kovac, Li–Tang, Conlon et al., Czenky et al., Korsky and the square-variant sketch are different questions. Kovac–Tang 2026 credits GPT-5.6 Sol with key proof steps, so assisted for that event, but it concerns best underapproximations, not this problem, and is a variant. The Lean statement and AlphaProof Nexus attempt contain no proof: none.
judgement.doubts: Louwsma–Martino 2025 was not read (PDF unreadable); its scope rests on a quoted abstract line, and it likely overlaps the 2023 preprint. Pihko 2001/2010 content rests on search summaries; the 2010 infinite family with numerators ending in 1 could arguably be read as a case, but it is pre-snapshot and does not change open vs open_stale. Korsky AI discrepancy unresolved but irrelevant here.
